title: Do You Have to Choose Between Happiness and Success?
metaTitle: Do You Have to Choose Between Happiness and Success?
metaDescription: No — research suggests happiness often comes before success, not just after it. The two tend to reinforce each other rather than trade off.
keyFinding: Happiness and success tend to reinforce each other rather than trade off — and research suggests happiness often precedes and contributes to success, not only the reverse.
honestAnswer: No — you generally do not have to choose, and the causal arrow may run opposite to what people assume. The common belief is that you grind first and happiness arrives later as a reward for success. But the research suggests happiness often comes before success and helps produce it, rather than waiting at the finish line — so the two tend to reinforce each other rather than trade off.

Two caveats keep this honest. It is a tendency, not a guarantee: happier people are not assured of success, and plenty of factors outside mood drive outcomes. And there is some evidence that the very highest levels of happiness are not optimal for every kind of achievement. But the headline holds — for most people, happiness and success are allies more than rivals.
whatDataShows: The influential review here is Lyubomirsky, King and Diener (2005), "The benefits of frequent positive affect: does happiness lead to success?", which synthesised a large body of cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental studies. Its broad conclusion was that happiness frequently precedes and contributes to success across domains — work, income, relationships, and health — not merely the other way around. Happier people tended, on average, to do better later, and experimentally induced positive mood improved relevant behaviours, which is harder to explain if success were the only cause.

The proposed mechanism is that positive emotion changes how people behave. Happier people tend to be more sociable, energetic, cooperative, and resilient, and to approach problems more flexibly — qualities that foster achievement over time. So rather than happiness being a payoff you collect after succeeding, it appears to feed the very behaviours that make success more likely.

Running the other direction, success alone is a weaker source of lasting happiness than people expect — a pattern often called the "arrival fallacy." Because of hedonic adaptation, the wellbeing bump from hitting a goal tends to fade as the achievement becomes your new baseline, which is why reaching the milestone you chased can feel strangely flat. So the trade-off framing gets it backwards twice: success doesn't reliably buy lasting happiness, and happiness helps produce success.
whyItFeelsDifferent: The sacrifice story is culturally dominant: work now, be happy later, as if happiness were a luxury you earn by suffering through the climb. That framing makes happiness and success feel like a zero-sum choice — time and energy spent on one as time taken from the other — when the evidence suggests they more often compound.

Adaptation also hides the reinforcing loop. Because the happiness gain from any single success fades, people conclude that happiness lives one milestone further on, and double down on grinding. They rarely notice that the cheerful, energetic state they treat as a reward-to-be-earned is itself part of what helped them get there.

And success is far more visible than the happiness that often preceded it. We see the promotion, the achievement, the outcome; we don't see the sociability, resilience, and flexible thinking that quietly fed it. So we credit the grind and discount the disposition, which makes the trade-off feel real even where the data points to mutual reinforcement.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Treat wellbeing as an input to performance, not only a reward for it. If happiness tends to precede success, then protecting the things that sustain it — relationships, rest, engagement, a sense of meaning — is not a distraction from achievement but plausibly part of what enables it. The framing shifts from "earn happiness by succeeding" to "sustain happiness and let it help you succeed."

Lean on the behaviours positive emotion tends to promote: connection, energy, cooperation, and resilience in the face of setbacks. These are the candidate mechanisms in the research, and they are worth cultivating directly rather than waiting for an achievement to grant them. You don't have to be happy first by luck — you can invest in the conditions for it.

And because success adapts away, don't bank your wellbeing on the next milestone. The research on the arrival fallacy suggests the satisfaction of hitting a goal is real but short-lived, so building a life you find good along the way — rather than deferring all of it to arrival — is the more reliable bet for both happiness and the sustained effort that produces success.
whatDoesNotHelp: Deferring happiness until after you succeed does not help, and may be self-defeating. The "be happy later" plan assumes success reliably delivers lasting happiness, but adaptation means the bump from any achievement tends to fade — so the finish line keeps moving, and the deferred happiness never quite arrives.

Sacrificing the sources of wellbeing — relationships, rest, health, meaning — in the name of achievement is not a clean trade. Since happiness appears to feed the sociability, energy, and resilience that foster success, gutting those sources can undercut the very performance the sacrifice was meant to serve.

At the same time, assuming maximum happiness guarantees maximum success is not supported either. Some evidence (e.g., Oishi and colleagues) suggests there may be an optimal rather than maximal level of happiness for certain outcomes, with the very highest levels not always best for achievement-oriented goals. So the honest claim is mutual reinforcement with limits — not that more happiness is always more success.
realNumbersInContext: The anchor here is a review rather than a single statistic: Lyubomirsky, King and Diener (2005) pulled together a large set of studies and concluded that happiness often precedes and contributes to success across work, relationships, and health — with experimental evidence (where mood is manipulated and outcomes measured) strengthening the case that the effect isn't only success causing happiness. As with any broad synthesis, effect sizes vary and the relationship is correlational in many of the underlying studies, so read it as a well-supported general pattern, not a precise number.

Two caveats sit alongside it. The arrival fallacy and hedonic adaptation explain why success alone is a weak and fading source of lasting happiness. And work such as Oishi and colleagues suggests an optimal-level qualification: the highest possible happiness is not always best for every achievement-related outcome. Net of all this, the evidence supports the idea that happiness and success reinforce each other rather than force a choice — without promising that either guarantees the other.

realNumbers.label: Review found happiness often precedes and contributes to success across domains
The 'arrival fallacy': success alone is a short-lived source of happiness due to adaptation
Highest levels of happiness may not be best for every achievement outcome

faqs.question: Do you have to sacrifice happiness to be successful?
faqs.answer: The research suggests not. The influential 2005 review by Lyubomirsky, King and Diener found that happiness often precedes and contributes to success across work, relationships, and health — not only the reverse. The two tend to reinforce each other rather than trade off, so the 'be happy later' sacrifice framing largely gets it backwards.

faqs.question: Does happiness actually cause success, or just come with it?
faqs.answer: Much of the evidence is correlational, but experimental studies — where positive mood is induced and outcomes measured — strengthen the case that happiness can help produce success, not only result from it. The likely mechanism is that happier people tend to be more sociable, energetic, and resilient, which fosters achievement over time.

faqs.question: Why doesn't reaching my goals make me as happy as I expected?
faqs.answer: This is often called the arrival fallacy. Because of hedonic adaptation, the wellbeing boost from hitting a goal tends to fade as the achievement becomes your new baseline — which is why reaching a milestone you chased can feel oddly flat. Success is a real but short-lived source of happiness on its own.

faqs.question: Is it possible to be too happy to succeed?
faqs.answer: There's some evidence for an optimal rather than maximal level. Work by Oishi and colleagues suggests the very highest levels of happiness aren't always best for every achievement-oriented outcome. So the honest picture is mutual reinforcement with limits — not a simple 'more happiness always means more success.'

faqs.question: So what should I actually do?
faqs.answer: Treat wellbeing as an input to performance rather than only a reward for it. Protect the sources of happiness — relationships, rest, engagement, meaning — and cultivate the behaviours positive emotion tends to promote, like connection and resilience. And don't bank your happiness on the next milestone, since its boost tends to fade.

dataSources: Lyubomirsky, S., King, L., & Diener, E. (2005). The benefits of frequent positive affect: Does happiness lead to success? Psychological Bulletin, 131(6), 803–855.
Brickman, P., & Campbell, D. T. (1971) — hedonic adaptation; and the 'arrival fallacy' concept (popularized by Tal Ben-Shahar).
Oishi, S., Diener, E., & Lucas, R. E. (2007). The Optimum Level of Well-Being: Can People Be Too Happy? Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2(4), 346–360.
